title: How do you teach good public policy-making?
transcript:
Host: How do you teach good public policy making? That's the challenge set by new graduates uh by a new graduate school in Sydney at a time when Australian civics education has fallen behind and trust in politicians and public institutions continues to fall. The University of New South Wales will launch its new graduate school of public policy at Old Parliament House tonight, offering what it calls a vocational first approach to the study of government. Rob Stokes is a former New South Wales State Government Minister and the advisory board chair for the new school at the University of New South Wales and joins me now. Rob Stokes, so welcome to breakfast.
Rob Stokes: Thanks, Ellie.
Host: Why do we need this?
Rob Stokes: It's so important because government is now so big and so complex. It's it's it's responsible for about 40% of spending in the Australian economy. And we need to make sure that everyone involved in government decision-making, from public servants to politicians, to policy advisors, to NGO leaders, everyone involved in making these decisions is appropriately trained in how to make it decisions effectively. And that's on the job training. We're not talking about 
a sort of theoretical approach, but very much practical, vocational and practitioner-led.
Host: So how do you teach that?
Rob Stokes: Uh well, you um there are whole range of different ways in which you can teach great public policy, but it's it's effectively about ensuring that you can translate what you're seeking to achieve to the decision-making forum in which those decisions are being made. Decisions on the floor of parliament are very different from decisions in a cabinet room or an expenditure review committee of cabinet or uh you know, in a party room or in uh in a departmental process. It's very important that people are scaffolded in understanding how these different processes work to ensure that decisions can be made efficiently. And I've seen this up close where um because people don't quite understand each other or because there's a level of naivety about how processes work, it can delay uh decisions about expenditure, which increases inefficiency, and actually increases the complexity of making decisions. When you're talking about hundreds of millions, if not billions of dollars, uh every dollar counts in terms of ensuring uh that the people making the decisions are more confident and better able to understand the processes by which they're made.
Host: A lot of those those coming into the public service hoping to occupy leadership roles come in through a graduate program in the department. Are those programs not already covering all of this?
Rob Stokes: This is quite different because uh a bit in the same way as UNSW established the graduate school of management um back in the 1970s, uh the university's seen a way in which we can help to contribute to what is a a wider social need, which is ensuring that not just the public service who have graduate schools uh internally are trained, but everyone else is trained in the same way, so that everyone involved in government decision-making, including the public service, who understand their own processes very well, but um you know, there there's always room to learn about decisions that are made uh within political processes as well. So that there's this piece of translation uh so that we can be more efficient because people can understand the different contexts in which decisions are being made. And and again, I can't stress. I've seen it personally where uh if there were if there was better understanding of decision-making processes, decisions could be made faster and uh and and people could could explain their way of thinking in a way that was was was fit for the for the purpose or the context of the decision-making forum.
Host: The relationship between government and the public service is is complicated. What have episodes like Robo debt taught us?
Rob Stokes: Uh well, precise I mean, firstly there's that I mean, I don't necessarily want to get into robo because that's just um, you know, such a such a such a catastrophic failure. Um, but, but, but I mean, that's just a headline one. I've seen up close a series of um, of of of examples um, from from issues that we were just discussing earlier, um, climate change and the failure of the cop negotiations, uh, whether in in it could also be um, other areas of um, sorry, I'm just being distracted by someone for a moment. Apologies. 
Um, it's so there's there's a whole range of of ways um, in in which um, government processes, sorry, there's someone just gesticulating at me. Apologies.
Host: You're all right? Um, just on a separate issue, in New South Wales, um, your former colleague and former leader Mark Speakman announced his retirement from Parliament last week. He warned that the party can't be labor light or one nation light. Is the party at risk of that in your view?
Rob Stokes: Yeah, so sorry, apologies. Apologies for that earlier. Um, yeah, look, I think um, uh, again, courses like this are important because they can ensure that um, public policy is made in a way that is transparent, that is understood, uh, and where 
sort of shrill extremes are exposed on the basis of, you know, making claims about government expenditure or outcomes that simply can't be delivered. Uh, again, it's it's all very easy for populists to scream from either side uh about the need to cut government programs. It's very incumbent then to determine, you know, what do you do instead? And a better understanding of public policy by those making it, uh, can ensure that uh, we are better governed. Uh, and it's all very easy when people are angry or upset, um, or when government seems to be failing us, uh, to point the finger at government itself. But the University of New South Wales is actually, instead, deciding, well, no, let's see what we can do to improve things. And I know many other universities are doing great work in this space. The difference of this public policy school is its inclusivity. It's not directed at politicians or at public servants or at staffers or at NGO leaders, but at all of them. And um we've taken very much our queue from international schools like the Kennedy School over in the United States or the Blavatnik School in the United Kingdom, uh and they've got great public policy schools uh with with global significance in that in those jurisdictions. It's high time that Australia had the same thing as well.
Host: Uh very briefly, the federal government is pushing Australia to become a global hub for AI and data centers, but there's a lot of public backlash. How do you get the balance right?
Rob Stokes: Well, again, I I strike back to the better uh educated and informed with with practical skills that our public that our policy makers are, the better decisions we're going to make in these sorts of areas. Uh and again, I I I'm speaking from from experience here. Uh when people feel confident uh about the message they are sending, uh and and confident in those decision-making forums, they're going to make better decisions. And when you're talking about such consequential issues and things like data centers aren't going to, you know, they're not going to have a consequence just now, but they are well into the future as well. So having that uh that scaffolded practitioner-led vocational focus on improving uh public sector and government decision-making is sorely needed.
Host: Rob Stokes, thanks for joining me this morning.
Rob Stokes: Thanks for having me. Sorry for the disruption.
